We examine this connection in a classification task inspired by synthetic aperture radar, where acquisition geometry determines a query for classifying unfocused spectral patches before image formation. Across small-scale spectral and radar-like tasks, aligned queries improve learning from limited data over parameter-matched circuits with mismatched or absent queries. These results provide a route from known spectral task structure to the design and validation of inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits.

title: Characterizing the Martin Luther King Event: Sun to Earth Evolution of the January 19, 2026 Geomagnetic Storm
abstract: We present a comprehensive Sun-to-Earth analysis of the extreme space weather event of 18 -19 January 2026, hereafter the Martin Luther King (MLK) storm, which produced a severe (G4) geomagnetic storm and one of the most intense solar radiation storms of Solar Cycle 25. The geomagnetic disturbance was driven by a fast Earth-directed coronal mass ejection (CME) associated with an X1.9-class flare from NOAA Active Region 14341. We combine multi-viewpoint remote-sensing observations, in situ measurements from Solar Orbiter and Wind, and physics-based magnetohydrodynamic simulations using the CORHEL-CME framework to reconstruct the eruption from the low corona to 1 au and identify the mechanisms governing its geoeffectiveness. Observations and simulations indicate that the eruption originated from a right-handed magnetic flux rope embedded in a complex magnetic environment dominated by a neighboring positive-polarity coronal hole. The simulations reproduce the observed CME morphology, asymmetric expansion, magnetic fields measured at both spacecraft, and Dst index evolution. The main discrepancy is attributed to filament material not included in the model. Favorable magnetic polarity alignment between the CME and coronal-hole field minimized magnetic erosion through interchange reconnection, enabling rapid escape and preservation of the strong southward magnetic field that drove the geomagnetic storm. The prolonged recovery phase resulted from interaction between the trailing CME and a following high-speed stream from the same coronal hole. These results demonstrate that storm intensity was primarily established by the coronal magnetic configuration, whereas storm duration was controlled by the ambient solar wind.

title: Diversity Without Labels: Task-Agnostic Coreset Selection Across Perception and Action
abstract: While data collection for model training is relatively easy, curating high-quality datasets from large collections is inherently challenging. Coreset estimation methods address this problem by identifying the best data subsets to train models on. However, existing approaches often require proxy model training, extensive annotations, or task-specific tailoring. Unsupervised alternatives typically exploit geometric properties in foundation model feature spaces, but are limited to pairwise image-to-image comparisons or comparisons against a fixed subset. We introduce CoreDNA, an unsupervised, task-agnostic coreset estimation approach that pools neuron activations from vision foundation models into per-image and per-dataset distributions. By comparing each image's distribution to the dataset-level distribution, CoreDNA can capture both low-level visual structure and high-level semantic information across layers. We find that high-quality samples concentrate in the tails of the last layer's activation statistics, which we validate by relating them to training-based coreset methods. Building on these findings, we develop a computationally efficient selection mechanism to construct task-agnostic, high-quality coresets for selective annotation and model training. Across image classification, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and imitation learning for end-to-end driving and mobile manipulation, CoreDNA matches or outperforms the state of the art, demonstrating unprecedented generalization across perception and action tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of compact activation-based representations for data selection.

title: Foundation-Model-Driven 3D Scene Graphs for Mobile Manipulation
abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.

title: ADA 2025: A Multimodal Dataset for Water-Deficit Stress Detection in Sugar Beets
abstract: Research and development into artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications in crop management are hindered by a lack of suitable public datasets. Whereas applications in disease and pest detection benefit from a comparatively higher amount of available data, applications like water-deficit stress detection often have very few if any public datasets available. Moreover, most datasets that are available are single-modality and frequently RGB-only, leaving the early detection and enhanced performance offered by other methods, and particularly by multimodal approaches, out of reach. Datasets with accurate metadata, higher numbers of plants, and smaller intervals between data points are also scarce. To address this, we publicly release ADA 2025, a >500 GB comprehensive multimodal dataset of young sugar beet plants under healthy and water-deficit conditions combining thermal, hyperspectral, RGB, and depth imagery along with relevant environmental and metadata and both relative water content (RWC) and leaf thickness as ground truth sources. Exemplary results showcase the dataset's validity in terms of differences detectable between stressed and healthy plants.

title: ShadowCast: On-the-Fly Context-Aware Shadow Augmentation for Remote Sensing Image Segmentation
abstract: Shadows cast by elevated objects alter the spectral appearance and obscure the boundaries of objects in remote sensing images, thereby degrading semantic segmentation performance. Most existing approaches handle shadows as degradations to be detected and removed, requiring additional costs from dedicated networks and shadow-specific annotations. We propose ShadowCast, which takes the opposite approach: it synthesizes shadows and injects them during training for remote sensing segmentation. It extracts masks of elevated objects, such as buildings and trees, directly from the segmentation labels and estimates an image-specific cast-shadow direction cue by probing the brightness around them. It then projects synthetic shadows along the inferred cast-shadow direction, requiring no learned network and no acquisition metadata. Experiments on three widely used remote sensing benchmarks, Vaihingen, Potsdam, and LoveDA, show that ShadowCast consistently outperforms the baseline across diverse state-of-the-art segmentation architectures. Moreover, it brings additional performance gains when combined with standard augmentation and regularization techniques, indicating that stochastic shadow injection serves as a simple and complementary augmentation strategy for remote sensing segmentation.

title: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction-driven perception through the "Embedding-as-Mask" paradigm. However, extending this capability to Remote Sensing (RS) reasoning segmentation remains exceptionally challenging under cluttered geographical contexts and extreme scale variations, often leading to Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long-form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.

title: FloodVLM-Pix: Language-Guided Pixel-Level Flood Understanding
abstract: As climate change intensifies, floods are becoming more frequent and destructive, making accurate flood understanding an urgent priority. However, existing vision-language models perform poorly on flood-related tasks, suffering from attentional bias and inaccurate descriptions of flood magnitude. To bridge this gap, we construct the first large-scale remote sensing flood multi-modal benchmark that supports language-level flood understanding and pixel-level flood segmentation. The benchmark contains 131,200 flood image patches and corresponding 443,100 textual descriptions for flood severity and evolution. Based on this benchmark, we propose FloodVLM-Pix, a language-guided pixel-level flood understanding model that includes a flood prior module and a multi-temporal flood pixel decoder to achieve accurate flood understanding. The flood prior module automatically distills sub-region flood spatial priors and inputs priors into FloodVLM-Pix, solving the attentional bias problem in flood language understanding. The flood pixel decoder introduces a novel general-specific feature fusion mechanism to address performance degradation caused by interference (e.g., clouds or mountain shadows) during flood segmentation. Experiments on FloodVL-Pix demonstrate that FloodVLM-Pix improves both flood description quality and pixel-level flood segmentation performance compared with state-of-the-art VLMs and flood segmentation models. Our code and data will be released at https://github.com/Haomiaoyanmeng/FloodPix.

title: Client-Aware Security Adaptive Early Exit Vision Transformers for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.

title: Understanding sub-arcsecond scale radio sources and space weather with the SKA-Low using interplanetary scintillation
abstract: Continuum surveys with SKA-Low will provide excellent spectral information for detected objects. However, the angular resolution it provides cannot clearly distinguish between extended radio galaxies and their sub-arcsecond scale counterparts. We have previously used an interplanetary scintillation (IPS) technique with wide field-of-view instruments (the MWA and ASKAP) to detect and study $<$0.3\arcsec\ objects. The ability to identify hundreds of compact sources from large areas of the sky using $<$5 minutes of data, and associated low computational cost makes widefield IPS a very efficient approach to identify sub-arcsecond scale objects at low radio frequencies. We aim to utilise SKA-Low's flexibility in data capture, frequency coverage and high sensitivity to develop widefield IPS technique with SKA-Low, enabling the identification of compact radio sources at angular scales more than an order of magnitude smaller than that achieved by SKA-Low's longest baselines. This capability will facilitate studies of compact source populations (e.g., AGN cores), their relationship to extended radio galaxies, AGN contributions in star-forming galaxies, identify candidates for pulsars and HI absorption, and provide a network of calibrators for direction-dependent ionospheric calibration for SKA-Low. Additionally, ground-based IPS observations are one of the very few remote sensing techniques to probe the Heliosphere which will enable SKA-Low to provide unique insights into the solar wind. Here, we present recent developments in the field of compact sources at low frequencies, their synergies with other fields of astronomy and space weather, and outline the technical developments and approaches that are necessary with the SKA-Low to realise these studies.

title: Local proxies for memory-efficient training
abstract: Local learning algorithms can reshape resource requirements of artificial intelligence. The memory bottleneck of standard end-to-end backpropagation lies in the need to store all network activations until the loss gradient has been propagated back through. Local learning avoids this, but typically at a cost in accuracy. We study how to achieve accurate and memory efficient local learning in transformers. For each transformer block, we train a local proxy network to predict the global network output via distillation. Gradients can be independently propagated through this local proxy while estimating well the backpropagation gradients. In theory, this approach is exact for deep linear networks; in non-linear residual models, the gradient error can be bounded when using the appropriate residual proxy. We verify this numerically and demonstrate that optimizing the distillation loss improves gradient estimation. Evaluating the performance of proxy propagation on CIFAR-100 in vision transformers, we find that it achieves a better accuracy/memory trade-off compared to other local algorithms. Finally, we show that the method is further relevant for fine-tuning large language models on a small memory budget. Our method trains faster and achieves higher performance than memory-efficient zeroth-order learning algorithms with comparable memory cost.

title: SpikeQ: Spike-Guided Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Neural Networks
abstract: On neuromorphic chips, spiking neural networks (SNNs) consume far less energy than artificial neural networks (ANNs), but the limited memory of these chips requires low-bit synaptic weights and membrane potentials. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods provide them without retraining and, like those for ANNs, minimize numerical errors such as the mean squared error (MSE). In an SNN, however, a quantization error reaches later layers only through the spikes it flips. We find that errors of equal MSE can cause very different accuracy losses, whereas errors that flip the same fraction of spikes cause the same loss. We therefore propose SpikeQ, a spike-guided PTQ framework. For weights, we select the level of each weight by simulating the downstream neurons and minimizing their spike errors. For membrane potentials, most existing methods quantize the state after the reset, whereas neuromorphic chips compare the threshold with the membrane potential stored at a fixed bit width. We target this pre-fire quantization and build a reset-aware grid that places the threshold on a rounding boundary, so rounding never flips the spike at the current time step. We evaluate SpikeQ on seven benchmarks of image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. With 2-bit pre-fire membrane potentials, every existing grid collapses, whereas SpikeQ retains most of the full-precision accuracy. With both at 4 bits, the models stay within 2.59 points of full precision, shrink their memory footprint 7.8--7.9 times, and use 6.4--6.9 times less energy.

title: MaskMerge: Structure-aware Token Merging for Efficient Instance Segmentation
abstract: Token merging improves the efficiency of Vision Transformers by combining redundant tokens, but existing methods largely rely on feature similarity to determine which tokens to merge. This criterion is effective for semantic segmentation, yet can fail in instance segmentation, where adjacent objects of the same class often have highly similar features. We identify this failure mode as cross-instance token fusion. We introduce MaskMerge, an instance-aware token merging method that uses coarse intermediate mask predictions to constrain feature-based merging and preserve instance boundaries. We evaluate MaskMerge on two diverse instance segmentation domains characterized by high inter-instance visual similarity: PanNuke and iSAID. Against the SOTA token merging method ALGM, MaskMerge improves mAP from 30.1 to 32.1 on PanNuke while reducing computation from 229 to 153 GFLOPs and running 1.18x faster, and from 33.1 to 36.2 on iSAID while reducing computation from 198 to 182 GFLOPs and running 1.23x faster. Additionally, we also test it on Cityscapes and match ALGM's performance while using fewer FLOPs. The gains also transfer to an MAE pretrained backbone, demonstrating that instance-aware merging enables more aggressive compression when appearance similarity alone cannot reliably preserve object identity.

title: Immersive Focus+Context Techniques to Assist in Interpretation of High Density Forest Point Clouds
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is changing how we interact with complex spatial datasets. VR has the potential within forestry to help analyse remotely sensed spatial data for inventory management. However, challenges of scale and legibility of dense forest point clouds must be addressed. To do so, we present three VR Focus+Context (F+C) techniques: Wedgelight, Remote Lantern, and Ray Lantern. These techniques present point cloud data using a constrained highdetail focus within a broader abstracted context representation, manipulated using egocentric and exocentric interactions. We conducted two user studies. The first informed the design of the F+C techniques. The results from the first study indicate that VR significantly outperforms desktop displays in basic analysis of forestry point clouds, with improvements to both time and accuracy. The second study evaluated the performance of the resulting F+C techniques in a task analogous to real-world forestry operations. Our F+C techniques significantly outperformed current approaches, confirming their viability for facilitating detailed and effective forest assessments. These findings indicate that VR has significant advantages for spatial data analysis tasks in forestry, making a strong argument for its adoption in future analytical frameworks. The F+C visualisation techniques we introduced show considerable promise for analysis of high density point clouds, opening new avenues for development in immersive analytics. Supplemental materials (code, scans, results) are available at https://osf.io/hqc9u.

title: CLARO: Clutter Aware Robot Orchestrator for Open-Vocabulary Grasping using VLM Agents
abstract: Robots that follow natural-language instructions unlock a wide range of autonomous applications in households, warehouses, and labs. Real-world environments are diverse and often heavily cluttered, requiring robots to plan over multiple steps, act, and replan as they work toward a goal. We present CLARO (CLutter-Aware Robot Orchestrator), a VLM agent that orchestrates a set of perception and manipulation skills: open-vocabulary object detection, segmentation, 6-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile pushing to locate and retrieve a language-specified target in clutter. CLARO maintains a memory of its past actions to support long-horizon execution, and emits manipulation targets (grasp poses/3D waypoints) allowing transfer across robot arms without task-specific training. We evaluate CLARO against a range of methods on a dynamic simulation environment and standard image-based benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization across object classes, lighting, and clutter levels. CLARO attains an average success rate of 89.1%, a relative improvement of over 16% on the strongest competing method in high cluttered scenes. We further analyze performance along grounding and grasping axes to characterize where each method succeeds and fails. Finally, we deploy CLARO on a robot arm across diverse cluttered scenes, achieving a success rate of 88.8%, and demonstrating strong sim2real generalizability.

title: Passive microwave sea ice concentration biases in the Southern Hemisphere revealed by ICESat-2 linear ice fraction
abstract: Gridded sea ice concentration (SIC) data are fundamental for understanding long-term polar climate. Since 1978, daily SIC data have been derived from passive microwave (PM) satellite observations. As SIC is not directly observed, it is obtained through an algorithmic inversion of PM brightness temperatures. Differences between PM-SIC algorithms lead to uncertainty in SIC data. Here we examine differences between several PM-SIC products and focus primarily on two: the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) Climate Data Record (CDR), which over our study period is derived from Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) data, and over the Southern Ocean is largely based on the Bootstrap (BT) PM-SIC algorithm, and the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR2)-based NASATeam2 (NT2) product. On individual days, changes in integrated Antarctic sea ice area (SIA) can reach as high as 1.6 million km 2 in summer with relative differences up to 37% at the annual sea ice minimum. Using more than 1.8 million coincident observations of the ICESat-2 Linear Ice Fraction (LIF) from 2018 to 2024, we find BT-based PM-SIC data underestimate Antarctic SIC by a median of 0.2 in areas classified as the marginal ice zone (MIZ), corresponding to a median relative difference in SIC of 31%. This offset is seasonally, spatially, and parametrically consistent and yields differences in apparent MIZ extent as high as 4.4 million km 2 . The offset exceeds reported CDR uncertainties that average 0.07 and cannot be explained as a consequence of sensor differences. The parametric simplicity of the observed bias means these offsets can be parameterized as a function of BT SIC alone, which could lead to an improved SIC dataset for Antarctic studies.

title: A revised model for atmospheric adjacency effect correction in optical satellite earth observation images
RT-ProtoNet: radiative-transfer-guided few-shot prototype networks for cross-region bathymetry in optically clear reef environments
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Satellite-derived bathymetry faces two coupled obstacles: labels are scarce, and models transfer poorly across regions. We propose RT-ProtoNet, a radiative-transfer-guided few-shot prototype network, which takes patches from three penetrating Sentinel-2 bands and treats ICESat-2 depths, aggregated to the 10 m grid, as sparse supervision; cross-region episodic meta-training then yields a transferable metric representation. Rather than embedding the radiative transfer relation as an analytic formula, we use it as a comparability criterion between support and query pixels, entering the attention as a learnable additive distance penalty. The prediction sums a convex combination over support depths and a base regression head trained on source domains only and frozen at deployment, so no target-domain parameters are estimated. We evaluate on five optically clear shallow reef regions by leave-one-region-out cross-validation against airborne laser bathymetry, against nine baselines, where K is the total number of support pixels (3, 5, 10, 20, 50). For K ≤ 20, RT-ProtoNet attains the lowest cross-region macro-mean RMSE (2.79–2.48 m), with a run-to-run standard deviation 0.67 times the runner-up’s; at K = 50, pre-training with head fine-tuning overtakes it. Ablation shows the residual head’s gain scales with support depth coverage (correlation 0.991) and that the two physical priors are largely substitutable; twelve perturbations to the attenuation input change RMSE by only 0.66%. The method suits depths of roughly 2–20 m and budgets of K ≤ 20, and does not extrapolate to turbid or optically complex waters. Independent evaluation at two external optical-domain sites, a moderately turbid embayment (Tampa Bay) and a clear-to-moderately-turbid transition site (Boquerón Bay), further delineates the method’s applicability across contrasting optical conditions, showing reliable transfer within the clear-water regime but substantial degradation under stronger optical attenuation.

title: UrbanQGS: Large-scale urban surface reconstruction via analytic curvature consistency in quadratic Gaussian splatting
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Large-scale 3D surface reconstruction at the city scale from UAV imagery is a core task for building digital-twin cities. Although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and its variants have achieved remarkable progress in radiance-field reconstruction, existing methods still struggle with scale-varying structural complexity and diverse urban textures: geometry is often incomplete in low-frequency, weak-texture regions over large areas, while in high-frequency regions with intricate details, disordered primitive distributions tend to cause floating artifacts and outliers. To address these issues, we propose UrbanQGS, a large-scale urban reconstruction framework built on quadratic Gaussian splatting. We inherit quadratic surface Gaussians as scene primitives and use their analytic curvature as the central driving signal to perform a two-stage geometric refinement: (1) A self-supervised geometric constraint based on cross-view curvature consistency, which effectively fills geometric holes in weak-texture planar regions. (2) A curvature-aware adaptive representation allocation strategy that reweights, recalibrates, and ranks densification gradients, guiding split and clone operations toward geometrically complex regions while standard pruning removes redundant primitives. In addition, we integrate a monocular normal prior to correct global orientation drift during large-scale reconstruction. We further assess the compatibility of UrbanQGS with partitioned large-scene reconstruction using a visibility-aware block-wise protocol with hardware-constrained per-block budgets. The blocks are trained sequentially on a single GPU. Experiments on large-scale UAV datasets demonstrate that, compared with state-of-the-art 3DGS-based large-scale reconstruction methods, UrbanQGS maintains superior geometric quality while substantially reducing redundant Gaussians and mesh complexity, yielding finer and more complete geometric structures, while qualitative results on our custom-collected dataset indicate its compatibility with a partitioned large-scene reconstruction pipeline.

title: N-PCLN: A physics-informed deep learning framework for short-term chlorophyll-a prediction with sparse satellite observation
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Chlorophyll-a (Chla) is a key indicator of lake eutrophication. Its short-term prediction is essential for water quality monitoring and bloom early warning. However, traditional deep learning models often rely heavily on dense observations and provide limited process interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a physics-informed deep learning framework, named N-PCLN, for short-term Chla prediction in Erhai Lake. The framework integrates Sentinel-3 OLCI imagery and meteorological datasets from 2016 to 2024. It uses Chla, land surface temperature, wind speed, and precipitation as inputs. Total phosphorus is incorporated through a nutrient–phytoplankton model to construct a physical loss. This design enables the model to jointly learn spatiotemporal patterns and nutrient–phytoplankton process constraints. The N-PCLN outperforms ConvLSTM, Transformer, MDN, CNN, and LSTM models, achieving an R 2 of 0.767, an MAE of 1.483 mg/m 3 , and an RMSE of 2.665 mg/m 3 . Sparse-data experiments show that N-PCLN maintains more stable performance than the selected baseline models under reduced data availability. The ablation experiments indicate that LST is the dominant meteorological factor driver of short-term Chla dynamics, while wind speed and precipitation mainly affect hydrodynamic redistribution and runoff-related nutrient transport. Physical-loss gradient analysis further reveals that the N-P constraint acts differently across seasons and Chla concentration. These results demonstrate that N-PCLN improves both prediction performance and process interpretability. It provides a useful framework for satellite-based lake water quality prediction.

title: Assessing the spatio-temporal cumulative drought effects on two Mediterranean forest types in Central Chile
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Droughts are long-lasting events that can drive persistent functional changes in ecosystems, particularly in drought-prone areas like Mediterranean forests. We integrated a phenology-based anomaly method, combining kernel density estimation (KDE) with cumulative sums (CUSUMs) to assess long-term drought impacts on two Mediterranean forest types in Central Chile. Using MODIS Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), the Moisture Stress Index (MSI), and Evapotranspiration (ET) from 2000 to 2024, we quantified cumulative deviations in canopy productivity, moisture conditions, and energy exchange. Our framework revealed persistent negative functional trajectories preceding the well-documented 2010–present megadrought. Spatially explicit metrics identified coherent degradation hotspots in northern sclerophyllous and southern deciduous forests, where canopy greenness, moisture, and evapotranspiration declined synchronously. Seasonal models indicated a post-2010 strengthening of soil–water controls over forest functioning, with soil moisture and water storage variables becoming influential predictors. The convergence of cumulative negative EVI, MSI, and ET signals highlights widespread and sustained functional weakening under prolonged drought conditions. Our results demonstrate that integrating KDE-derived anomalies with cumulative deviation tracking provides a sensitive and transferable framework to detect early and persistent vegetation stress in water-limited ecosystems.

title: Deep learning detection of submesoscale eddies from MODIS SST in the South China Sea
abstract: Submesoscale eddies play crucial roles in oceanic energy cascades and material transport; however, their detection faces substantial challenges owing to inadequate spatial resolution in traditional satellite altimetric measurements. This research introduces Sub-Eddy-Net, an innovative deep learning approach utilizing an enhanced YOLOv8-SGAM architecture for identifying submesoscale eddy features within MODIS-derived sea surface temperature (SST) imagery across the South China Sea region. By exploiting SST data's advantageous temporal coverage and observational continuity relative to altimetric sensors, synthetic aperture radar, and ocean color products, the developed algorithm demonstrates detection precision of 0.968, successfully identifying 20,443 submesoscale eddies throughout 2015–2024. Results indicate cyclonic eddy prevalence exceeds anticyclonic occurrences, exhibiting average radii of 13.1 km and 13.7 km respectively. Eddy distributions primarily cluster within coastal waters and Luzon Strait vicinity, displaying pronounced seasonal patterns. Comparison with Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) observations shows 64.3% matched features, 27.1% positional offsets, and 8.6% detected only in SST. Within the same eddies, coherent chlorophyll-a (Chla) signatures were present in a smaller fraction, indicating that SST is the more robust tracer for systematic detection. This Sub-Eddy-Net methodology offers a scalable approach for examining submesoscale oceanic phenomena, providing a decadal inventory for further study of their roles in ocean circulation and vertical exchange.

title: Is a Linear Probe Evidence of a Linear Representation?
abstract: The linear representation hypothesis holds that pretrained vision models encode generative factors as linearly decodable directions in feature space, and comes with a standard methodology: train a linear probe, declare a factor represented if accuracy is high. We show this test is too permissive. Asymptotically, any sufficiently rich feature map, including a random one, admits a linear readout, so high probe accuracy is consistent with two very different geometries: a true linear world model, where the latent-aligned subspace dominates the representation, or a kernel machine, where the latents lie linearly inside a much larger curved manifold. This distinction matters because the curved structure orthogonal to the probe is relevant for out-of-distribution generalization, robustness, and compositional transfer. We propose three asymmetric diagnostics that distinguish the two cases: reverse predictivity, spectral concentration, and out-of-distribution generalization. We validate them in a fully observed simulation where ground truth is known. Applied to six pretrained vision transformers on SVG-World, our deterministic generative benchmark with paired visual styles, and to two of them on CelebA, they show pretraining produces structure beyond a random kernel but well short of a linear world model. On dSprites, 3D Shapes and MPI3D, forward decodability and latent-aligned variance dissociate. Thus, forward decoding alone does not show that the probed factors align with the dominant geometry of the representation. In summary, our work cautions about the success of linear probes as opposed to truly linear and low dimensional representations.

title: Integrating Landsat and ECOSTRESS to explore the value of additional thermal infrared satellite observations for field-scale evapotranspiration mapping
abstract: Landsat has provided an indispensable foundation for field-scale evapotranspiration (ET) mapping but is constrained by its overpass temporal frequency. Although integrating additional thermal data offers a pathway to bridge this gap, the magnitude of improvement varies across observation characteristics and surface context and remains less understood. Here, ECOsystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (ECOSTRESS) is used as an additional thermal source on top of the Landsat baseline to evaluate the value of more frequent thermal observations for improving field-scale ET time series. We implemented a Google Earth Engine -based Disaggregated Atmosphere-Land Exchange Inverse + Data Mining Sharpener framework to generate a Landsat-based ET baseline and enhanced it with ECOSTRESS observations. The resulting ET data was validated across 25 flux-tower sites spanning diverse land-cover types and climate zones across the contiguous United States. When integrated with Landsat, the addition of ECOSTRESS observations reduced interpolation errors and improved temporal consistency across most sites. However, improvements in ET time series agreement depended strongly on (1) the extent to which ECOSTRESS reduced effective Landsat sampling gaps and (2) the accuracy of overpass-day ECOSTRESS ET retrievals. Improvements were largest when ECOSTRESS shortened Landsat observation gaps by ~50% and maintained high scene quality. ECOSTRESS overpass time also influenced performance, with acquisitions between 10:00–14:00 producing most reliable ET estimates. These results support developing methods with multi-satellite observations to strengthen field-scale ET and help address the key knowledge gap regarding the value of increased thermal observations.

title: Twin-satellite constraints from GF-5B and DQ-1 enable hourly near-surface NO2 estimation across China
abstract: Nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) is a major air pollutant with significant impacts on human health, yet satellite-based estimates of surface NO 2 with full diurnal coverage remain limited. Here, we develop a machine learning framework to estimate hourly near-surface NO 2 concentrations across China by integrating complementary observations from two Chinese polar-orbiting satellites, GF-5B (~10:30 local time) and DQ-1 (~13:30 local time). A Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model driven by twin-satellite NO 2 vertical column densities (VCDs) and meteorological reanalysis achieves strong predictive performance in 10-fold cross-validation, with a coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.91 and root mean square error (RMSE) of 5.40 μg/m 3 across all hours (4.46 μg/m 3 during daytime; 6.32 μg/m 3 at night), and retains reasonable skill under stricter site-based, time-based, and independent cross-year validation. The reconstructed dataset captures the characteristic diurnal cycle of NO 2 , with morning and evening peaks associated with traffic emissions and a midday minimum driven by photochemical loss. Compared to the single-satellite TROPOMI product, the twin-satellite configuration substantially improves the representation of diurnal variability, increasing R 2 from 0.81 to 0.91 and reducing RMSE by 31.60%, and corrects a distorted urban-rural NO 2 exposure ratio (1.70 for TROPOMI versus a ground-based 1.19), narrowing it to 1.30. Feature-importance analysis further shows that meteorological variables dominate model predictions during both day and night, with satellite VCDs providing a complementary, though indirect, constraint on nighttime concentrations. The resulting hourly NO 2 dataset demonstrates the value of synergistic multi-satellite observations for air quality monitoring and provides a robust basis for refined pollution control and population exposure assessment.

title: Advanced characterization of the diurnal variations of aerosol optical and microphysical properties by SYREMIS/GRASP synergistic retrieval algorithm using observations from multiple spaceborne sensors
abstract: Accurate characterization of the diurnal variation of aerosol optical and microphysical properties—including Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), Angstrom Exponent (AE), and Single Scattering Albedo (SSA)—is fundamental for climate and air quality modeling. However, retrieving high-temporal-resolution, physically consistent aerosol products from multiple satellite instruments remains a challenge. Current multi-satellite approaches often rely on “post-retrieval” merging of independent Level-2 products, a process that frequently introduces physical inconsistencies and artificial temporal oscillations. To address this, building upon the recently established SYREMIS/GRASP synergetic retrieval framework (Litvinov et al., 2025), an inversion approach based on harmonized Level-1 satellite measurements, this study extensively evaluates its performance in capturing aerosol diurnal variability. We evaluate two configurations: (i) LEO + LEO synergy (Sentinel-3 A/B OLCI and Sentinel-5P TROPOMI) and (ii) LEO + GEO synergy (integrating Himawari-8 AHI). By enforcing multi-pixel smoothness constraints within the retrieval, SYREMIS maintains high physical consistency across instruments, effectively mitigating the structural discrepancies and “noise” inherent in standard merging techniques. Our validation against AERONET ground-based data and intercomparison with the XAERDT product suite confirm that SYREMIS provides high retrieval stability and accuracy. Without applying post-retrieval quality filtering, SYREMIS achieves an AOD GCOS fulfillment percentage of up to 70%, an AE RMSE below 0.3, and an SSA “Optimal” requirement fulfillment rate of up to 85% at representative sites. We demonstrate the framework's capability to resolve rapid aerosol dynamics through case studies of biomass-burning events over Thailand and Myanmar, as well as dust pollution over Qatar in 2019. As a three-month proof-of-concept assessment (March–May 2019) , these results highlight the practical capability of the established SYREMIS/GRASP approach to generate high-resolution, physically consistent, and stable aerosol data records from the measurements of multiple satellites.

title: Constructive solid geometry for automatic topology-aware BIM reconstruction from point clouds
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: The automatic reconstruction of Building Information Models (BIMs) remains challenging, especially when applied to multi-storey buildings and indoor environments with non-Manhattan layouts and curved structures. To address these challenges, this paper presents a novel method that places Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) at the core of building reconstruction from point clouds. The methodology also integrates the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and knowledge-based rules to reconstruct as-built BIMs while preserving the geometry and topology of building elements. The proposed approach consists of two main stages: SAM-based segmentation and CSG-based modelling. First, SAM is used to segment rooms, as well as door and window openings. Solids are then generated for the indoor spaces and openings. Finally, a set of Boolean operations is applied to reconstruct building elements, including slabs, walls, indoor spaces, doors, and windows, while subtracting openings of doors, windows, and staircases. Finally, the reconstructed model is encoded with semantic information following the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema. The method was evaluated on seven two-storey building point clouds and demonstrated strong performance, achieving a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) greater than 90% for floor plan reconstruction, a precision above 87% for door and window detection, and mean geometric deviations below 8 cm for BIM reconstruction.

title: SkySplat++: Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting for generalizable sparse-view reconstruction from multi-temporal satellite imagery
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Scene reconstruction from sparse-view satellite images remains a challenging task due to insufficient geometric constraints. While generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods have shown high efficiency for novel-view synthesis, existing methods are often unsuitable for satellite imagery due to incompatibility with the rational polynomial coefficient (RPC) model and limited generalization capability. In this work, we present SkySplat++, a hierarchical generalizable 3DGS framework that extends our previous SkySplat to further improve scene reconstruction. SkySplat++ refines Gaussians in a coarse-to-fine manner, enabling robust modeling of both large-scale scene structures and fine-grained texture details. To improve reconstruction under sparse-view conditions, a Height-Guided Hierarchical Cost Volume (HG-HCV) module is integrated to enable more accurate cost volume construction. Additionally, a hybrid height supervision strategy is employed to stabilize height estimation under radiometric inconsistencies. Compared to per-scene optimization methods, SkySplat++ achieves up to 36 times speed up over EOGS through feed-forward inference after training, while achieving higher accuracy. It also outperforms generalizable 3DGS baselines, reducing mean absolute error by 10.38–14.81 m relative to HiSplat across two benchmarks, and demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization on the MVS3D test set. The code will be released at https://nancheng2001.github.io/SkySplatV2/ .

title: A GeoAI framework for remote-sensing-driven traffic activity and emission intensity in a data-scarce megacity
abstract: In rapidly expanding megacities across the Global South, a profound data scarcity paradox frequently prevents effective environmental monitoring and evidence driven urban planning. While severe traffic congestion generates acute localised pollution, the total absence of continuous municipal traffic counters, ubiquitous vehicle telemetry, and air quality monitoring networks leaves these environments empirically unmonitored. This study resolves this challenge by introducing a reproducible geocomputational framework designed to map microscale traffic activity and relative emission landscapes by fusing multisource geospatial data and deep learning workflows. Focusing on the unmonitored context of Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, our methodology uses very high resolution 15 cm satellite imagery to train and deploy a localised YOLOv8 (You Only Look Once, version 8) computer vision model, establishing an empirical baseline of fleet distribution. These static counts are dynamically distributed across the urban road network using a probabilistic Hub and Spoke Gravity Model, which is weighted through a zero shot Large Language Model semantic reclassification of unstructured OpenStreetMap features. Reconstructed kinematic flows are subsequently processed through velocity dependent Tier 3 EMEP/EEA algorithms to capture the nonlinear emission penalties triggered by severe network gridlock. To ensure framework defensibility, an independent unmanned aerial vehicle observation campaign was executed across ten distinct urban sites. The drone data directly validate model estimated physical parameters, achieving robust correlations for traffic volumes (R2 = 0.826) and link speeds (R2 = 0.925). Because literature derived chemical emission factors cannot be validated in situ, all absolute outputs are subjected to a rigorous multiparameter sensitivity analysis to report findings strictly as bounded ranges. The results reveal a clear structural handover in the spatial activity profile of the city. Daytime pollution is heavily driven by the informal paratransit fleet, which accounts for a bounded range of 82.8% to 95.1% of total PM2.5 emissions along primary corridors despite representing a numerical minority of active vehicles. Conversely, nocturnal baseline emissions transition to a landscape dominated almost entirely by private passenger vehicles. All code, processing pipelines, and validation datasets are available in a FAIR compliant open access repository. This framework establishes a scalable, remote sensing driven blueprint for diagnosing traffic activity structures in unmonitored metropolitan regions worldwide.

title: FasterAD: Faster and more precise multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection and localization
Self-promotion learning with label prediction and revision for SVM
TDCount: Thermal-only crowd counting for privacy-conscious deployment
VLKD-YOLO: A semantic-aware visual-language distillation framework for lightweight underwater object detection
Substantial disagreement between satellite- and ground-level nighttime light patterns revealed by SDGSAT-1 and street view imagery
abstract: Over the past three decades, nighttime light (NTL) has become one of the most widely used and powerful proxies for characterizing human activities. Despite the recent proliferation of available NTL data from both satellite- and ground-level sensors, intrinsic differences between these two observation approaches can result in distinct NTL brightness patterns (satellite-ground disagreement). Such disagreement, particularly its spatial heterogeneity, represents a critical yet largely overlooked issue in NTL studies, introducing uncertainty into the interpretation and application of NTL observations. Here, by incorporating SDGSAT-1 glimmer imagery and panoramic nighttime street view imagery with geospatial AI approaches, we present a spatially explicit, wall-to-wall investigation into satellite-ground disagreement across Singapore. Specifically, we characterized citywide disagreement and its variation across land-use types, analyzed contributing factors, and assessed its implications for NTL-based applications, reinforced by Monte Carlo-based uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analyses using independent observations from Singapore and Shenzhen, China. Our study revealed substantial and spatially heterogeneous satellite-ground disagreement across Singapore. Relative disagreement averaged 15% ± 13% citywide but reached 42% ± 12% in 13% of the city. Such pronounced heterogeneity was likewise evident across land-use types, with commercial areas standing out for consistently significant disagreement, where ground-level NTL brightness was 29% ± 26% higher than satellite-level NTL brightness. Building morphology, vegetation canopy cover, and sensor spectral response contributed to satellite-ground disagreement, suggestive of distinct mechanisms underlying the identified patterns. Applying satellite- and ground-level NTL data yielded relative differences of at least 115% and 83% in GDP estimation and NTL exposure inequality assessment, respectively. This study sheds new light on satellite-ground disagreement by moving beyond discrete comparisons toward a comprehensive analysis of its heterogeneity and implications, thereby establishing an empirical basis for integrating NTL observations and contributing to more reliable NTL-based applications and evidence-informed policies on sustainable urbanization.

title: Evaluating multi-satellite VIIRS active fire observations as a burned area proxy across North America
abstract: Wildfire activity fundamentally regulates terrestrial carbon dynamics and atmospheric emissions, necessitating timely and spatially complete mapping of burned area. Traditional reflectance-based burned area products provide robust spatial records but often have multi-week to multi-month processing latencies that limit near-real-time applications. Active-fire detections provide low-latency observations, but their use as a burned area proxy is constrained by temporal sampling gaps and commission errors associated with sub-pixel fire detection. This study represents one of the first applications to use the full three-satellite Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) constellation, comprising S-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21, to address these limitations. Here, we evaluate how the spatial performance of a cumulative VIIRS active-fire approach varies with temporal sampling, latitude, and fire regime. We developed a VIIRS Cumulative Active Fire (VCAF) approach using the 375-m VIIRS active-fire record across North America from 2012 to 2024, and evaluated its spatial agreement with visually interpreted reference labels and the North American Fire History (NAFH) dataset, using MCD64A1 as a benchmark burned area product. Results from the first full year of the three-satellite configuration (2024) indicate that VCAF had higher spatial agreement than MCD64A1 in parts of the high-latitude domain (>50°N), with particularly high patch-level recall for small reference burned patches (<100 ha) while maintaining high recall for large patches (>1000 ha). The observed performance varied substantially with latitude and fire regime. In high-latitude boreal regions, the greater potential sampling frequency of the VIIRS constellation was associated with lower omission errors and greater spatial completeness in some regions, although environmental conditions such as persistent cloud cover remained important limitations. In contrast, VCAF systematically overestimated burned area in fragmented lower-latitude fire regimes. These results indicate that multi-satellite VIIRS active-fire observations can provide a potentially useful burned area proxy in selected high-latitude fire regimes and highlight the importance of accounting for temporal sampling and fire-regime characteristics when interpreting active-fire-based burned area estimates.

title: Divergent transpiration regulation among 20 urban tree species under extreme heat revealed by UAV multisource remote sensing
abstract: Urban areas face increasing extreme heat risk, yet satellite remote sensing struggles to quantify crown-scale transpiration in heterogeneous urban landscapes. Consequently, species-specific heat responses, key regulatory factors, and tipping points of urban tree transpiration remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) multispectral, thermal infrared, and LiDAR observations with field surveys of 665 trees across 20 species to estimate crown-scale transpiration for nearly 50,000 trees. The UAV-based single-source energy balance model captured diurnal evapotranspiration (ET) dynamics and agreed well with eddy covariance measurements (R 2 = 0.86, RMSE = 0.04 mm h −1 ). At the individual-tree scale, UAV-derived crown-scale transpiration agreed closely with sap-flow-derived transpiration (R 2 = 0.88, RMSE = 0.05 mm h −1 ) and leaf area index (LAI)-upscaled portable-photosynthesis-system transpiration estimates (R 2 = 0.88, RMSE = 0.06 mm h −1 ). Compared with the normal day, landscape ET was higher on the extreme-heat day, mainly reflecting higher tree transpiration (0.47 vs. 0.40 mm h −1 ), whereas grassland and shrub ET remained relatively stable. At the species level, three event-specific response groups were identified: enhanced with significantly higher transpiration under extreme heat (12 species), neutral with no significant change (3 species), and suppressed with significantly reduced transpiration (5 species). Random forest analysis identified the temperature vegetation dryness index (TVDI) and leaf-to-air vapor pressure deficit (VPD L ) as dominant controls of crown-scale transpiration, with tree height (TH) also exerting a strong influence. SHAP-derived tipping points for TH were identified at 7.01, 4.42, and 3.65 m in the enhanced, neutral, and suppressed response groups, respectively. SHAP-derived tipping points for TVDI (0.23–0.34) and VPD L (5.34–5.84 kPa) suggested the transition toward soil-water limitation and atmospheric-demand regulation. Overall, this framework enables spatially explicit assessment of urban tree water use and provides a basis for species selection and irrigation management during extreme heat.

title: DynamicVis: Dynamic visual perception for efficient remote sensing foundation models
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: The continuous advancement of remote sensing technology has enabled high-resolution Earth observation; however, interpreting these expansive images using modern Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) remains a significant challenge. Unlike object-centric natural images, remote sensing imagery is fundamentally characterized by extreme target sparsity and massive spatial redundancy. Key objects of interest (e.g., ships, vehicles, scattered buildings) often occupy less than 1% of the spatial extent, surrounded by vast, target-free backgrounds. Many existing VFMs rely on uniform dense processing (e.g., Vision Transformers), while a substantial branch adopts pixel-reconstruction pre-training paradigms (e.g., Masked Autoencoders). These designs may waste substantial computational capacity on modeling redundant backgrounds and dilute the feature representations of small, sparse targets. To bridge this structural misalignment, we propose DynamicVis , a remote sensing visual foundation model explicitly tailored to spatial sparsity in high-resolution imagery, with a focus on large-scale visual pre-training and transferable spatial representations for diverse downstream perception tasks. Architecturally, DynamicVis introduces a Dynamic Region-Aware State Space Model (SSM) that bypasses uniform computation. It adaptively routes and incrementally models only task-relevant, high-salience tokens while employing a parameter-free integration for background context, drastically reducing the complexity of processing ultra-long 2D token sequences ( ∼ 100,000). Crucially, to equip the network with robust spatial-selection capabilities, we propose a novel weakly supervised Region-Level Meta-Embedding Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) pre-training paradigm. Trained on a million-scale dataset, this paradigm promotes foreground-aware regional discrimination in the latent semantic space, mitigating the semantic ambiguity of conventional pixel-reconstruction methods. Extensive evaluations across nine diverse downstream visual perception tasks reveal that DynamicVis achieves competitive performance across region-, instance-, and pixel-level remote sensing tasks, with particularly strong results in sparse-target and instance-level perception tasks (e.g., small object detection and instance segmentation). Notably, DynamicVis processes high-resolution imagery (2048 × 2048) with merely 97 ms latency and 833 MB of memory consumption without employing any acceleration techniques (approximately 6% and 3% of a base ViT, respectively), offering a favorable trade-off between computational scalability and representation accuracy for multi-granular remote sensing analysis. Source code is available at https://github.com/KyanChen/DynamicVis .

title: Global cross-modal geo-localization: A million-scale dataset and a physical consistency learning framework
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Cross-modal Geo-localization (CMGL) matches ground-level text descriptions with geo-tagged aerial imagery, which is crucial for pedestrian navigation and emergency response. However, existing studies are constrained by narrow geographic coverage and simplistic scene diversity, failing to reflect the immense spatial heterogeneity of global architectural styles and topographic features. To bridge this gap and facilitate universal positioning, we introduce CORE, the first million-scale dataset dedicated to global CMGL. CORE comprises 1,034,786 cross-view images sampled from 225 distinct geographic regions across six continents, offering an unprecedented variety of perspectives in varying environmental conditions and urban layouts. We leverage the zero-shot reasoning of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) to synthesize high-quality scene descriptions rich in discriminative cues. Furthermore, we propose a physical-law-aware network (PLANET) for cross-modal geo-localization. PLANET introduces a novel contrastive learning paradigm to guide textual representations in capturing statistical scene descriptors of satellite imagery. Extensive experiments across varied geographic regions demonstrate that PLANET significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, establishing a new benchmark for robust, global-scale geo-localization. The dataset and source code will be released at https://github.com/YtH0823/CORE .

title: Physics-driven semantic scattering structure understanding of aircraft target in SAR images
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) has become indispensable for target interpretation owing to its all-day and all-weather observation capability. In SAR target interpretation, electromagnetic scattering information provides a physically grounded cue beyond visual texture and has been widely exploited for target interpretation. However, existing methods remain dominated by local scattering center representations. Such unordered and component-agnostic representations are highly unstable for aircraft targets. As a result, physically existing components with weak scattering responses are often missed, resulting in the incomplete reconstructed topology structure. To address this limitation, we establish Semantic Scattering Structure Understanding as a new paradigm for SAR aircraft interpretation. Semantic scattering keypoints are defined to associate local electromagnetic responses with physically meaningful aircraft components, while visibility-aware attributes are introduced to retain weakly observable yet physically existing components. The keypoints are further organized into a stable semantic scattering structure. Building upon this, we propose S 3 U-SAR, a physics-driven framework to localize semantic scattering keypoints and construct the complete representation constrained by multi-dimensional physical priors, including scattering heterogeneity, rigid-body topology, speckle uncertainty. A confidence-gated joint supervision strategy is further introduced to alleviate optimization conflicts. We construct KP-SAR-Aircraft-1.0, the first fine-grained benchmark for semantic scattering structure understanding. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S 3 U-SAR achieves the best performance compared with baselines. Class-disjoint cross-category and cross-dataset evaluations further verify its generalization capability and transferability. Notably, in downstream orientation estimation, the method improves P 1 ° and P 5 ° by 15.0% and 19.1% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed representation paradigm in advancing SAR target understanding from implicit local response regression toward explicit global structural representation. The trained model and dataset will be available at https://github.com/YYF121/S3U-SAR .

title: Breaking modal barriers: Achieving modality-balanced semantic segmentation across optical and SAR images through optical image-supervised learning
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: As the two primary imaging modalities in remote sensing, optics and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) have been widely applied in semantic segmentation tasks. However, the scarcity of annotated samples in SAR images limits the performance of related models. How to leverage the abundant annotated samples of optical images to achieve modality-balanced semantic segmentation capabilities across both optical and SAR modalities is of great significance for all-weather interpretation. Restricted by the complexity of modality perception, achieving balanced cross-modal segmentation still faces significant challenges. To address the above issues, we fully consider the modal balance and reliability of knowledge transfer in modal migration and propose a modality-balanced knowledge distillation (MBKD) transfer learning framework. By generating and learning virtual modalities and stitched modalities, a cross-modal migration task is transformed into two symmetric intra-modal migration subtasks, explicitly promoting balanced knowledge transfer between modalities. To demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed framework, we conducted application experiments on the large-scale public dataset WHU-OPT-SAR, MULTISENGE-6, and in 6 provinces of China. The results show that our method significantly outperforms other approaches in terms of both performance and stability.

title: GeoSeg-SAM: Task-aligned adaptation of SAM for geological remote sensing interpretation
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) has shown strong performance in natural image segmentation. However, its direct transfer to geological environment remote sensing (GERS) is limited by significant domain discrepancies. GERS elements typically exhibit high class diversity, strong inter-class similarity, and imbalanced sample distribution, which challenge SAM’s prompt-driven paradigm in maintaining semantic stability and spatial contextual consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose GeoSeg-SAM, a geological task-aligned adaptation framework built upon SAM. GeoSeg-SAM progressively aligns generic visual features with geology-discriminative semantics through layer-wise semantic adapters, and introduces a dual-scale structure-aware module in the deeper encoder layers to enhance global region-level contextual representation. Meanwhile, the model employs Pyramid Residual Aggregation (PRA) to fuse multi-level geological semantic representations across stages, thereby improving the representational capacity of features. In addition, at the mask prediction stage, decoded features are fused with PRA-based semantic representations using a semantics-constrained fusion decoding strategy, and a single geological semantic token is incorporated to enhance semantic consistency in GERS scenarios. Experimental results on three representative GERS study areas show that GeoSeg-SAM improves mIoU by approximately 3 percentage points or more over the best competing method in each area, confirming its effectiveness in GERS image interpretation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/WanZhan-lucky/GeoSeg-SAM .

title: MCHex: marching cubes based adaptive hexahedral mesh generation with guaranteed positive Jacobian
abstract: Grid-based methods are robust for automatic hexahedral (hex) meshing, but struggle with boundary fidelity and element quality. Conventional pipelines remove outside elements, yielding axis-aligned surfaces converging to the input geometry at first order; subsequent padding and projection are heuristic, offering no guarantees on final boundary fidelity or mesh quality. This paper introduces MCHex, a fundamental reformulation of boundary and mesh-quality handling in grid-based hex meshing. MCHex applies marching cubes (MC) inside each grid cell, ensuring the mesh boundary is an MC surface. The key insight is that constraining cut-cell configurations to 3-regular polyhedra and applying midpoint subdivision produces an all-hex mesh with guaranteed positive Jacobian for every element. MCHex provides three advantages: (1) theoretical positive-Jacobian guarantee for every element; (2) boundary convergence matching MC’s approximation rate, via a non-heuristic algorithm with well-bounded time complexity and the fastest wall-clock time among existing methods; and (3) manifold surfaces for arbitrary geometries plus a natural padded layer. Extensive evaluation on 202 benchmark geometries, using a slightly smaller element budget, compares MCHex with previous state-of-the-art methods; it consistently yields positive-Jacobian meshes with similar boundary fidelity while running significantly faster. It integrates seamlessly with post-processing such as smoothing and simplification, and is suitable for simulation.

title: 3D HyFormer: A hybrid transformer with dense-sparse attention for point cloud semantic segmentation
A3AD: Enhancing CLIP with Triple-Aware Learning for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
A decade of summer glacier fronts and calved glacier ice distribution in Kongs- and Krossfjorden, Svalbard, observed by Sentinel-1 extra wide swath
abstract: A statistical method to map atmospheric exposure is applied on the whole decade (2015–2024) of Sentinel-1 summer acquisitions in Extra Wide Swath mode over Kongs- and Krossfjorden on Svalbard. The consistent daily observations not only allow to statistically define a summer glacier front extent of marine-terminating glaciers but also reveal a new application, which is to detect the summer distribution of calved glacier ice, i.e. icebergs, bergy bits and growlers (IBG). These originate from glacier calving during the sea-ice free period. Summer glacier extent that we define statistically as the area where the glacier prevails more than 95% during summer co-locate well with independent glacier fronts digitized from Sentinel-2 optical imagery. Annual summer IBG distributions are classified into percentage ranges of temporal occurrence, representing the proportion of time IBG are detected in the corresponding pixel location. The ten-year record of mean annual summer IBG-occupied areas is compared to separate estimates of summer glacier frontal ablation for the two glaciers Lillehöökbreen and Kronebreen. The comparison indicates a clear link between mean summer calved ice distribution area and the glaciers' frontal ablation with correlation coefficients (r) of 0.67 and 0.85 for Lillehöökbreen and Kronebreen, respectively. Frontal ablation includes both calving and submarine/subaerial melting at the glacier front and combining this with IBG occurrence estimates may provide new insights into the mass loss ratio between calving and melting. However, the relationship between IBG occurrence distribution and frontal ablation appears to be glacier specific. As this study represents a first attempt to map IBG occurrence distribution and mean IBG occupied area and link that to glacier frontal ablation, further studies and application on other glaciers and fjord systems are required to fully assess the potential and limitations of mapping such IBG distribution as a proxy for glacier calving intensities.

title: From national to global: Mapping global center-pivot irrigated cropland with knowledge-guided data augmentation
abstract: Center-pivot irrigated cropland (CPIC) is a large-scale, intensive agricultural irrigation practice with high water-use efficiency. This characteristic enables CPIC to increase crop yields and promote agricultural development, while simultaneously causing groundwater overexploitation and subsequent environmental issues. Mapping the global distribution of CPIC is critical for enhancing water resource management, guiding agricultural policies, and assessing ecological impacts. This study developed a novel methodological framework integrating CPIC prior knowledge into the generation of a global training dataset through designed algorithms, ultimately producing a 2020 global CPIC map (GCMap) based on Landsat imagery. Specifically, we first proposed a shape-prior guided Projection Simulation (PS) to enhance the diversity of national-scale CPIC samples, enabling global CPIC pseudo-label generation through a teacher model. Subsequently, a stratified sampling strategy was implemented to improve sample representativeness across different regions using the pseudo-labels of global CPIC. Furthermore, a dual-temporal correction mechanism was proposed to clean sample labels, ultimately generating high-confidence global training samples. Finally, based on this dataset, a student model was trained using a noise-resistant loss function and deployed on cloud computing platforms to generate the GCMap rapidly. Following Olofsson's design-based stratified sampling and error-matrix framework, we derived statistically rigorous area estimates with explicit 95% confidence intervals and assessed mapping accuracy using the corresponding user's accuracy (UA), producer's accuracy (PA), and overall accuracy (OA) metrics. In comparison with current CPIC products, our GCMap attained a PA of 0.86 ± 0.02, representing a marked reduction in omission errors. Our results show that the global error-adjusted area of CPIC in 2020 was estimated at 18.70 ± 0.42 Mha, representing a 63% increase relative to the previous estimate of 11.5 Mha and revealing substantial underestimation in previous estimates. Geographically, the semi-arid zone has the largest share of CPIC, covering 9.27 ± 0.29 Mha (49.28% of the total), followed by the arid zone (4.69 ± 0.20 Mha, 24.95%) and humid zone (2.99 ± 0.22 Mha, 15.92%). Further analysis indicates that most CPIC is distributed in aquifers with limited underwater recharge. Approximately 15.25 ± 0.87 Mha (82.04%) of CPIC areas are located in regions with recharge rates below 100 mm/year, of which 9.97 ± 0.48 Mha (53.62% of total CPIC) fall within extremely low recharge zones (<20 mm/year). These findings provide an essential foundation for further research on irrigation-groundwater interactions and sustainable policymaking about agricultural development and water usage. Our GCMap inventory is publicly available in an online repository at: https://doi.org/10.12436/GCMap.62.20250711 .

title: GeoPhysAdapter: Scale-matched geophysical adaptation for cross-domain landslide mapping with vision foundation models
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Newly triggered landslides rarely carry immediate annotations, so cross-domain transferability determines the value of landslide mapping for emergency response and regional risk assessment. Vision foundation models have strengthened representational transfer, yet on unseen regions, events, and sources they still generate high-confidence false alarms. Terrain, material, and rainfall triggering can constrain such errors, but their supports are local, regional, and event-scale, so resampling onto a 10 m grid misaligns them with the segmentation decision unit and compounds the uncertain geographic context problem (UGCoP). We propose GeoPhysAdapter, which anchors on a frozen vision foundation model, restricts terrain, material, and triggering to dense spatial guidance, regional modulation, and event-timing forcing, and applies bounded adaptation at two decision units, the pixel and the candidate landslide body, reverting exactly to the visual prediction where support is insufficient. On an event-isolated PILD dataset of four public sources, 55 global landslide events, and 7890 test samples, 70.3% of cross-domain false-positive mass lies in near-pure spurious bodies of median equivalent diameter 207 m, matching coarse-prior support rather than the pixel. Pixel-level adaptation removes a net 507,817 erroneous pixels, reducing error by 7.76%, whereas raising the decision unit to the candidate body, under identical samples, anchor, and baseline, increases error reduction to 23.99% and improves IoU by a relative 14.2%. The gain decreases monotonically with terrain displacement, exceeds a strong optical control of spectral change and visual confidence alone by 0.019 IoU, remains positive across five vision anchors, and survives a pre-registered re-execution with a 20.61% error reduction. The binding constraint is therefore the match between the native scale of physical priors and the operative decision unit, not denser physical stacking. Data and code are publicly available at https://github.com/Liu-Zhihang/geophysadapter .

title: Cross-sensor continual maritime object recognition via spectral shift modulation in heterogeneous infrared–visible UAV imagery
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Multi-modal maritime object recognition is pivotal for UAV-assisted search and rescue. However, large-scale multi-platform UAV deployments inevitably encounter heterogeneous infrared sensors with diverse spectral response functions, leading to non-stationary multi-modal distributions and severe dynamic spectral shifts across successive multi-platform UAV deployment phases. Existing continual learning paradigms typically focus on mitigating catastrophic forgetting via memory replay, but overlook the sensor-specific biases inherent in spectral variations. Such biases induce negative transfer and performance degradation, as the model fails to decouple stable object features from dynamic spectral fluctuations. To address these challenges, we propose C3SM, a cross-sensor spectral shift modulation framework. The core of C3SM is a design-inspired spectral shift parsing prior that decouples sensor-specific spectral responses from sensor-invariant structural cues. By anchoring the fusion features to a structure-consistent reference space within the spatial-frequency domain, the proposed prior quantifies the cross-sensor discrepancy into a spectral shift index. Leveraging this proxy index, C3SM integrates a prior-guided cross-sensor memory modulation module. This module stabilizes the continual learning trajectory by adaptively suppressing unreliable high-shift memory experiences. Furthermore, a shift-robust contrastive learning strategy enforces feature alignment across spectral shift clusters, ensuring the capture of robust cross-sensor correlations. Extensive evaluations on the UAVSensorCL dataset across four heterogeneous sensors illustrate that C3SM achieves a 48.88% mAP at 7.15 FPS, outperforming state-of-the-art CODA-Prompt-PL (45.92% mAP) and ER-PL (45.09% mAP). By mitigating spectral interference, C3SM provides a robust baseline for maritime object recognition across dynamic environments. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Dingyuan-Chen/C3SM .

title: Integrating multi-source physical knowledge into deep learning for satellite soil moisture downscaling
abstract: Fine-resolution soil moisture (SM) is essential for understanding land–atmosphere interactions and managing hydrological hazards at local scales. Passive microwave remote sensing provides reliable SM observations but is limited by its coarse spatial resolution. Spatial downscaling offers an important means of addressing this limitation. However, many existing downscaling methods either rely on physical models with over-simplifications of soil hydrological knowledge, or data-driven models (particularly Deep Learning, DL) that lack interpretability, while current physics-guided DL approaches often emphasize a limited number of physical relationships or constraints. In response, this study proposes a framework to integrate multi-source physical knowledge into DL for satellite SM downscaling. Specifically, the framework incorporates physically informed drivers, a DisPATCh-informed physical regression branch, a hydrologically motivated consistency loss, and a constrained SM boundary loss, while using a gating module to adaptively fuse physically guided and data-driven representations. Evaluations based on in-situ and aircraft SM observations, together with coarse-scale consistency checks against SMAP SM, show that the proposed framework can effectively downscale SMAP SM from 9 km to 500 m. Using region-specific models across ten environmentally diverse regions, MPhy achieved station-averaged Pearson’s R and ubRMSE values of 0.76 and 0.05 m3/m3, respectively; the corresponding values for the pure-DL baseline Dens were 0.68 and 0.06 m3/m3. Detailed experiments in WGEW further showed that MPhy generally performed better than the pure-DL baseline, DisPATCh, single-physics-informed models, and selected conventional machine-learning methods.
